(Today through Tuesday)...
Issued at 131 AM EDT Wed Oct 14 2026

Today Through Thursday.

An approaching upper-level shortwave trough over the northern Plains 
will flatten the downstream ridge, forcing a surface cold front to 
sag southward into central Indiana through the day. Gulf moisture 
will pool along and ahead of this boundary, driving PWAT values 
upward into the 1.4 to 1.7 inch range, which sits well above the 
90th percentile for mid-October.

As of early this morning, elevated showers associated with the 
aforementioned moisture advection continues to move across northern 
Indiana and portions of Illinois. These showers may impact the 
northwestern counties, but otherwise expect convection to hold off 
until later in the day. Modest mid-level lapse rates will limit 
buoyancy with model soundings showing a skinny CAPE profile, but 
with SBCAPE values of 500 to 1200 J/kg updrafts will be strong 
enough to allow for thunderstorm development. Effective bulk shear 
around 35 to 45 kt will provide sufficient organization for 
multicell clusters and isolated transient supercell structures. The 
primary convective threats will be localized damaging wind gusts and 
brief torrential rainfall, though widespread severe weather is not 
expected given extensive cloud debris limiting stronger diurnal 
heating.

The frontal boundary will decelerate and oscillate across the region 
tonight as an open shortwave ejects northeastward from the middle 
Mississippi Valley. This will at least some convection through the 
overnight, but much less than during the daytime hours.

On Thursday, a deeper, amplifying mid-latitude trough over the Upper 
Midwest will induce surface cyclogenesis along the frontal wave, 
dragging a secondary, stronger cold front across central Indiana 
Thursday afternoon and evening. Pre-frontal warm sector recovery 
will support renewed thunderstorm development. While shear profiles 
remain strong with 0-6 km bulk shear exceeding 50 kt, thermodynamic 
profiles will be conditionally dependent on morning cloud clearance. 
Any pockets of surface heating will enhance low-level lapse rates, 
maintaining an isolated strong-to-severe risk along and ahead of the 
frontal line before dry slotting and strong cold advection scour out 
precipitation from west to east Thursday night.

Friday Through Tuesday.

A sharp pattern transition will occur Friday in the wake of the cold 
frontal passage as a broad, amplified longwave trough settles over 
the eastern half of the CONUS. Robust low-level cold air advection 
will cause 850mb temperatures to tumble from near +10C Thursday 
evening to between -2C and -4C by Friday afternoon. Efficient 
boundary layer mixing in steep low-level lapse rates, combined with 
a tight surface pressure gradient behind the departing surface low, 
will generate sustained northwest winds of 20 to 25 mph with 
frequent gusts of 30 to 40 mph Friday afternoon. Lingering 
stratocumulus under the cyclonic upper flow will keep daytime highs 
capped in the upper 50s.

A sprawling 1028-1030mb surface high pressure will build from the 
northern Plains into the lower Ohio Valley over the weekend. 
Diminishing winds and clearing skies Friday night will yield lows in 
the upper 30s but winds should remain just elevated enough through 
the night to avoid frost formation outside of very sheltered areas.

The primary frost and freeze concern arrives Saturday night into 
early Sunday morning. The surface ridge axis will center directly 
across central Indiana, setting up optimal conditions for 
radiational cooling with calm winds, a clear sky, and surface 
dewpoints dropping into the low 30s. Both deterministic GFS/ECMWF 
runs and the EPS/GEFS ensembles indicate high confidence in 
overnight lows dropping into the lower 30s across most of the area, 
with subfreezing minimums possible likely in traditional cold 
drainage areas. Frost headlines will likely be required for this 
period. 

By Monday and Tuesday, the upper-level trough will lift into the 
Canadian Maritimes as low-amplitude ridging and quasi-zonal flow 
overspread the mid-Mississippi and Ohio Valleys. The surface high 
will shift toward the mid-Atlantic coast, establishing southerly 
return flow. Low-level warm air advection will drive 850mb 
temperatures back toward +8C to +10C, allowing daytime temperatures 
to moderate into the upper 60s and lower 70s. Subsidence under the 
surface ridge will ensure dry conditions across central Indiana 
through Tuesday ahead of the next upstream disturbance.
